conceptTag: Cash at an agency with late-paying clients
readerTitle: Profitable every month, short on payroll by Friday
caseNote: 가상 사례 (디자인 에이전시, 금속 가공 공장) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 에이전시의 현금 문제는 매출이 아니라 일한 날부터 돈 받는 날까지의 시간 문제이고, 그 시간은 대부분 계약할 때 정해진다.
misconception: 이익이 나고 있으니 현금은 따라온다. 현금이 부족하면 고객을 더 늘리면 해결된다.

sources.text: 관리회계·재무관리의 표준 개념 (현금 순환 주기, 매출채권 회수)

factChecks.note: 에이전시 월 손익: 청구액 $80,000 − 인건비·임대료 $65,000 = 월 이익 $15,000. 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
타임라인: 1일 작업 시작 → 30일 비용 $65,000 지급 및 $80,000 청구 → 60일 지급 기한(30일 조건) → 105일 평균 입금. 비용 지급(30일)부터 입금(105일)까지 75일. 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5개월분 비용을 늘 회사 돈으로 부담한다는 단순화입니다.
조기 결제 할인, 지연 이자, 매출채권 금융의 조건과 적법성은 나라마다 다르므로 구체적 비율이나 법적 내용은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Profitable every month, short on payroll by Friday
body: Your design agency has eight people. It made a profit every month this year, about $15,000 a month on paper.
Today the bank shows $22,000. Payroll and rent, $65,000, are due Friday. Meanwhile, clients owe you more than $200,000.

image.label: Agency owner looking at a low bank balance beside a tall stack of unpaid invoices
image.brief: 작은 디자인 스튜디오 책상. 노트북 화면에 낮은 잔액 "$22,000", 옆에 높게 쌓인 미수 청구서 더미에 "Unpaid $200,000" 태그. 벽 달력의 금요일에 "Payroll" 동그라미. 실제 은행·회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: Your biggest clients pay 60 to 90 days after you invoice. You need to get through Friday and stop this from happening every quarter.

options.text: Open a bank credit line to cover payroll
options.feedback: It gets you through Friday, but it only rents cash. Your **cash cycle** stays just as long, and now you pay interest on it.

options.text: Call the clients with the oldest invoices today, then change how you bill new work
options.feedback: This handles Friday and the cause. **Getting paid on time** is something you build into the deal, not a favor you ask for later.

options.text: Win two more clients to bring in more money
options.feedback: More clients means more payroll now and more cash later. With a long **cash cycle**, growth digs the hole deeper before it fills it.

cards.title: Follow one month of work.
body: The profit is real. It just arrives **75 days** after the money to earn it went out.

breakdown.label: $65,000 out
breakdown.detail: Payroll and rent paid; $80,000 invoice sent

breakdown.label: Invoice due
breakdown.detail: Terms say 30 days. Most clients haven't paid

cards.title: The cash cycle
body: The **cash cycle** is the time between paying out cash and getting it back from customers. A furniture store's cash sits in sofas. An agency's sits in hours of work it has already paid for.
Here the cycle is 75 days. So the agency always carries about two and a half months of costs from its own pocket. The monthly profit doesn't help until it lands.

image.label: Timeline with money leaving on day 30 and returning on day 105
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 30일 지점에서 빨간 화살표로 "$65,000 out", 105일 지점에서 초록 화살표로 "$80,000 in". 두 지점 사이를 "75 days your cash is away"라는 넓은 띠로 강조.

cards.title: What clients owe you at any moment
body: When clients pay 75 days after the invoice, about two and a half months of billing is always unpaid. Get them to 30 days and **$120,000** comes back into the bank, without one new sale.

groups.label: Owed to you, by days to pay

cards.title: Getting paid on time
body: Most late payment is set up at the start of a project. For an agency, the fixes go into the proposal and the contract:
list: **Deposit at signing:** part of the fee before work begins
**Bill as you go:** monthly or by milestone, not at the end
**Invoice the same day** work is approved, with the due date clear
**One named owner** who checks invoices before they're late
cards.callout: Each step shortens the cash cycle from the collection side.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies do this with annual plans paid upfront and cards charged automatically. Cash arrives before most of the cost of serving the customer.

cards.title: Big clients write their own terms.
body: A large company may insist on 60 or 90 days. Pushing too hard can cost you the account. Early-payment discounts work, but they come straight out of your margin.
When terms won't move, the honest fix is to price the wait into your fee, and to line up enough cash or credit to cover the cycle before you sign.

cards.title: Now it's a machine shop.
body: You run a 20-person shop making metal parts. A large equipment maker offers a contract that would double your sales at a good margin.
You buy steel upfront and pay staff weekly. They pay 90 days after delivery. What do you do?

options.text: Sign it. A profitable contract pays for itself
options.feedback: Profit isn't cash. Doubling sales on 90-day terms doubles the money tied up in steel, wages and unpaid invoices, which can empty the bank before the first payment arrives.

options.text: Sign, but ask for a material deposit or staged billing, and arrange credit for the gap first
options.feedback: You win the work and size the **cash cycle** before it starts. **Getting paid on time** here means agreeing when cash moves, not just the price.

options.text: Turn it down. 90 days is too long
options.feedback: It protects your cash but gives up a strong customer. A long cycle is a cost to plan for and price in, not always a reason to walk away.

cards.title: Profit that hasn't arrived can't pay anyone.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **The cash cycle** showed how long your money is away. **Getting paid on time** showed how to bring it back sooner, mostly by deciding when cash moves before the work begins.
**Try it today:** list every unpaid invoice with its age. Call about the oldest one, and add a deposit to your next proposal.
